# Inspecting the record a one-shot run left behind

Both one-shot modes finish in the invocation that started them and leave a
durable artifact directory. An operator reads that record afterwards, without
re-running anything, by serving its state through an ordinary deployment and
querying it with the same verbs and routes any deployment answers.

## The manifest one-shot

A manifest with a mixed roster — one instance succeeds, one fails.

`rimsky-compose.yml`:

```yaml
project: audit-artifact

templates:
  - path: ./template-success.yml
    tag: succeed
    state: deployed
  - path: ./template-failure.yml
    tag: fail
    state: deployed

instances:
  - template: succeed
    name: ok
  - template: fail
    name: oops

executors:
  peer:
    transport: grpc
    endpoint: "127.0.0.1:9091"
```

`template-success.yml` (the failure template is the same with
`outcome: fail`):

```yaml
name: audit-artifact-success
version: "1"
message_queue_mode: backlog
nodes:
  - type: worker
    executor: peer
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          outcome: {type: string, default: ok}
          echo: {type: string, default: success-leg}
```

Run it, binding the executor to a local binary:

```bash
rimsky compose run --service peer=/path/to/peer-host ./rimsky-compose.yml
```

The invocation finishes the run. It exits 1 for the mixed roster and reports
each leg by name:

```
audit-artifact/ok: success
audit-artifact/oops: failure
```

It leaves `.rimsky/latest` pointing at a run directory holding `state.db`,
`blobs/` and the `rimsky.yml` the run used. The executor process the run spawned
is gone.

## The ad-hoc one-shot

`rimsky run` self-hosts a template with no manifest.

```yaml
name: audit-artifact-adhoc
version: "1"
message_queue_mode: backlog
nodes:
  - type: okworker
    executor: peer
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          outcome: {type: string, default: ok}
          echo: {type: string, default: adhoc-success-leg}
  - type: failworker
    executor: peer
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          outcome: {type: string, default: fail}
          echo: {type: string, default: adhoc-failure-leg}
```

```bash
rimsky run --service peer=/path/to/peer-host ./template.yml
```

Same shape: exit 1 for the mixed outcome, and its own artifact directory holding
the whole record.

## Read the record back

Copy the run's `state.db` into a deployment's state directory and start it.

```bash
mkdir -p ./serve && cp .rimsky/latest/state.db ./serve/state.db
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -v "$PWD/serve:/var/lib/rimsky" rimsky-all-in-one:<tag>
export BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

Then query it:

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/instances"
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/events?instance_id=$IID&limit=200"

rimsky instance get "$FAIL_IID"    --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
rimsky instance nodes "$FAIL_IID"  --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
rimsky instance events "$FAIL_IID" --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
rimsky node get "$NODE_ID"         --endpoint "$BASE" -o json

curl -sS "$BASE/v1/observability/nodes/$OK_IID/worker"
```

## What the product does

Both instances are in the record and both are terminal. The event stream replays
`terminal/success` for the succeeding leg and the failure's own error class for
the other — for a third-party executor that refuses, `terminal/error/third-party/refused`.
The succeeding leg's attribute writeback is readable through the observability
node view. Two consecutive reads return the same event count: reading the record
does not disturb it.

The choice between the two one-shot modes does not cost the audit trail. Both
leave a record an operator can debug and verify from.
